timeline.title: Born in Bonn
timeline.text: Ludwig was baptised in Bonn on 17 December 1770. His birthday is usually given as 16 December, which he accepted himself, but only the baptism is recorded. His grandfather had been the court Kapellmeister, and his father Johann was a court singer.

timeline.title: A first concert
timeline.text: His father gave him hard, strict music lessons from a young age. In March 1778 the boy played in public for the first time. His father advertised him as six, though he was seven.

timeline.title: Neefe, his teacher
timeline.text: In 1780 or 1781 he began lessons with the court organist Christian Gottlob Neefe, his most important teacher in Bonn. Neefe helped him write and publish his first works.

timeline.title: First published music
timeline.text: A set of keyboard variations (WoO 63) became his first published work. Three piano sonatas followed the same year.

timeline.title: A paid court musician
timeline.text: After working without pay as assistant organist from 1782, he became a paid member of the court chapel in 1784.

timeline.title: A short trip, a sad return
timeline.text: In spring 1787 he visited Vienna for about two weeks. He hurried home, and his mother died in July, soon after he got back.

timeline.title: Head of the family
timeline.text: His father was forced to retire because of his drinking. Half of his father's pension was paid to Ludwig instead, so he could support his two younger brothers.

timeline.title: To Vienna
timeline.text: Haydn met him in Bonn and agreed to teach him. In November 1792 Beethoven moved to Vienna for good, and studied counterpoint with Haydn until 1794. His father died soon after he left Bonn.

timeline.title: Vienna hears him
timeline.text: He made his public debut in Vienna at the Burgtheater, playing a piano concerto. The same year his three Piano Trios, Op. 1, were published and sold well.

timeline.title: The First Symphony
timeline.text: At a concert he organised himself at the Burgtheater, his First Symphony was played for the first time.

timeline.title: A secret told to friends
timeline.text: In letters to his friends Wegeler and Amenda he admitted he was losing his hearing, with a constant ringing in his ears. He later said it began around 1798. The cause is not known for certain.

timeline.title: The Heiligenstadt Testament
timeline.text: On his doctor's advice he spent the summer in the village of Heiligenstadt. There he wrote a long letter to his brothers about his despair at his deafness, and about his resolve to live on for his art. He never sent it. It was found among his papers after he died.

timeline.title: The Second Symphony
timeline.text: He conducted the premiere of his Second Symphony, written mostly at Heiligenstadt in the same months as the Testament. It is full of energy and good humour.

timeline.title: The Eroica
timeline.text: His Third Symphony had its first public performance. He had first named it after Napoleon, and reportedly tore up the title page when Napoleon crowned himself emperor. Twice as long as a usual symphony, it opened his bold middle period.

timeline.title: An opera that failed
timeline.text: His only opera opened while French troops occupied Vienna, to nearly empty houses. It was a failure. He did not give up on it and began to revise it.

timeline.title: The Violin Concerto
timeline.text: Franz Clement played the premiere, reportedly sight-reading part of it because the solo was finished so late. It was rarely played until a 12-year-old Joseph Joachim revived it in 1844.

timeline.title: One famous concert
timeline.text: At the Theater an der Wien he presented the Fifth and Sixth Symphonies, the Fourth Piano Concerto and the Choral Fantasy for the first time, in one long, under-rehearsed concert.

timeline.title: Paid to stay
timeline.text: When he was offered a post in Kassel, three noble patrons promised him a yearly income to stay in Vienna. That spring Napoleon's army besieged the city as he finished his Fifth Piano Concerto.

timeline.title: Summer in Teplitz
timeline.text: In the spa town of Teplitz he met the poet Goethe and finished his Seventh and Eighth Symphonies. There he also wrote a love letter to an unnamed "Immortal Beloved". Who she was is still disputed.

timeline.title: The Seventh Symphony
timeline.text: He conducted the premiere at a charity concert for soldiers wounded at the Battle of Hanau. The audience demanded the slow second movement again at once.

timeline.title: Fidelio, at last
timeline.text: After two rounds of revision, his opera returned as Fidelio and this time was a success. It is the version performed today.

timeline.title: A guardian
timeline.text: His brother Kaspar died. Beethoven fought Kaspar's widow in the courts for years over the care of his nine-year-old nephew Karl. He won custody in 1820.

timeline.title: Talking on paper
timeline.text: His hearing was now so poor that visitors wrote their side of a conversation in notebooks. These conversation books survive from 1818 on. The same year he finished the huge Hammerklavier piano sonata.

timeline.title: Custody won
timeline.text: After long legal struggles he regained custody of his nephew Karl. He was also deep in work on the Missa solemnis for his pupil and patron Archduke Rudolph.

timeline.title: The Ninth Symphony
timeline.text: The Ninth Symphony, ending with a choir singing Schiller's Ode to Joy, was first played at the Kärntnertortheater. Beethoven, almost fully deaf, stood on stage beside the conductor. The singer Caroline Unger reportedly turned him round to see the applause he could not hear.

timeline.title: The late quartets
timeline.text: He turned to string quartets, partly for a commission from Prince Galitzin. After a month ill in bed in spring 1825, he wrote a slow movement he called a holy song of thanks for his recovery.

timeline.title: The last finale
timeline.text: It was a hard year at home, and his nephew Karl went through a serious crisis. At his brother's house in Gneixendorf, Beethoven wrote a new last movement for his Op. 130 quartet to replace the very difficult Grosse Fuge. It was the last work he finished.

timeline.title: Still planning
timeline.text: Ill in bed, he thanked the Philharmonic Society of London for a gift of money. He wrote that a tenth symphony lay fully sketched in his desk.

timeline.title: Death in Vienna
timeline.text: He died after months of illness, at 56. Doctors found serious liver damage. The exact cause of his death, like the cause of his deafness, is still debated.

timeline.title: The city says goodbye
timeline.text: About 10,000 people followed his funeral procession. He was buried in the Währing cemetery. Months later his Heiligenstadt Testament was published.

timeline.title: Beside Schubert
timeline.text: His remains were moved to Vienna's Central Cemetery and buried beside Franz Schubert.

timeline.title: The Beethoven-Haus
timeline.text: A citizens' association was founded to save his birthplace at Bonngasse 20. The museum opened in 1893 and now holds the largest Beethoven collection in the world.

timeline.title: A score for the world
timeline.text: UNESCO added his handwritten score of the Ninth Symphony, held by the Berlin State Library, to its Memory of the World Register. It was the first musical score to be listed. The Ode to Joy melody is also the anthem of Europe.

feature.title: The nine symphonies
feature.lead: Beethoven wrote nine symphonies over about 24 years, most of them while his hearing failed. Each one tried something new, and together they changed what a symphony could be.

items.label: No. 1 in C major, Op. 21
items.text: It opens with chords that seem to be in the wrong key, so the home key arrives slowly. The minuet is played so fast it is really a scherzo.

items.label: No. 2 in D major, Op. 36
items.text: Written mostly at Heiligenstadt as his deafness grew, yet bright and energetic. He replaced the old minuet with a lively scherzo, and its musical jokes surprised critics.

items.label: No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55, Eroica
items.text: About twice as long as a symphony by Haydn or Mozart, with three horns and a finale of variations and fugue. It was first meant for Napoleon. It is often called the first Romantic symphony.

items.label: No. 4 in B-flat major, Op. 60
items.text: A lighter work between two giants. It begins with a hushed, mysterious slow introduction in the minor before breaking into bright B-flat major.

items.label: No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67
items.text: Built on a four-note short-short-short-long idea that returns all through the work. The third movement runs straight into the finale, where trombones, piccolo and contrabassoon join in for the first time in his symphonies.

items.label: No. 6 in F major, Op. 68, Pastoral
items.text: Five movements instead of four, each with a title about life in the country: a brook, birdcalls, a peasant dance, a storm. He called it more the expression of feeling than painting.

items.label: No. 7 in A major, Op. 92
items.text: Driven by strong, repeated dance rhythms. First played at a charity concert for wounded soldiers, where the slow Allegretto was encored. Wagner called it the apotheosis of the dance.

items.label: No. 8 in F major, Op. 93
items.text: His shortest symphony, about 25 minutes, full of humour and sudden accents. He called it his little symphony in F. It looks back to the old minuet, while its finale is the weightiest movement.

items.label: No. 9 in D minor, Op. 125, Choral
items.text: The first symphony by a major composer to use singers: soloists and choir sing Schiller's Ode to Joy in the finale. Written when he was almost fully deaf, its tune is now the anthem of Europe.

works.title: Piano Trios, Op. 1
works.text: Three trios for piano, violin and cello, dedicated to Prince Lichnowsky. His first works published in Vienna as Op. 1, and a financial success.

works.title: Symphony No. 1
works.text: His first symphony, premiered at a concert he organised himself in Vienna.

works.title: Piano Sonata No. 14, "Moonlight"
works.text: A sonata "in the manner of a fantasy", dedicated to his pupil Giulietta Guicciardi. The nickname "Moonlight" came later, from the critic Rellstab.

works.title: The Heiligenstadt Testament
works.text: An unsent letter to his brothers about his deafness and his decision to live for his art. Kept since 1888 at the State and University Library in Hamburg.

works.title: Symphony No. 3, Eroica
works.text: The huge symphony that began his middle period and stretched the form far beyond what Haydn and Mozart had done.

works.title: Violin Concerto in D major
works.text: Written for Franz Clement. Neglected at first, it is now one of the most important violin concertos.

works.title: Symphonies No. 5 and No. 6
works.text: Two very different symphonies, one stormy and one calm and pastoral, first heard on the same night.

works.title: Piano Concerto No. 5, "Emperor"
works.text: Finished during the siege of Vienna and dedicated to Archduke Rudolph. His hearing was too poor for him to play the solo himself. The nickname is not his.

works.title: Fidelio
works.text: His only opera: a wife disguises herself as a prison guard to rescue her husband from a political prison. It took him three versions, from 1805 to 1814.

works.title: Piano Sonata No. 29, "Hammerklavier"
works.text: One of the hardest piano works ever written, 40 to 45 minutes long. No one played it in public until Liszt in 1836.

works.title: Missa solemnis
works.text: A grand mass for Archduke Rudolph. On the score he wrote: from the heart, may it return to the heart.

works.title: Symphony No. 9, Choral
works.text: His last symphony, with a choral finale on Schiller's Ode to Joy. The autograph score is in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

works.title: The late string quartets
works.text: Five quartets and the Grosse Fuge, written in 1825 and 1826 when he was fully deaf. They are among the most searching music he wrote.

works.title: Letters
works.text: Hundreds of letters to friends, patrons and publishers survive, translated into English by Lady Wallace in 1866.
